Do not recapture every GIF or run unrelated native suites merely to make the change look rigorous. If the book builder changes, its own tests and actual rendered output are relevant; parser success alone is not layout review.

ND01 / A SECOND CONSOLE
A second console
What makes a second console more than another model?

The motivating question is not whether a DS-shaped object can sit on the desk. It is whether selecting it establishes a coherent cartridge, display, input and persistence boundary without disturbing the original console. The outcome of this chapter is a vocabulary for that boundary: what the implementation supports, what its first prototype established, and what neither a successful demo nor a product label can establish.
This account stops at implementation 61845372142b41992916f3732ea102cc0f4c8edf. It describes recorded evidence; authoring this chapter did not execute new emulator tests.
The prototype answered a deliberately smaller question

Workstream 79 requested playable Nintendo DS emulation beside the retained console, while keeping static hosting and separate runtime lifecycles. Its original technical result used pinned EmulatorJS 4.2.3/DeSmuME to boot the project's original Twin Lab homebrew without supplied BIOS or firmware. Real native frames reached both modeled LCDs; buttons and lower-screen stylus input reached the core. That was substantially more than a decorative screen animation. It was still a local prototype result, not a commercial compatibility matrix, physical-phone qualification or publication. [S1]

The distinction matters because the model and the runtime advanced at different rates. The first silhouette, disconnected hinge and loose pen-like stylus were rejected while verified emulator and save behavior were preserved. Remodeling the shell did not require throwing away the native integration. Conversely, native output did not make the first model visually acceptable. The historical record explicitly separates those outcomes rather than retroactively making the initial attempt successful in every dimension. [S1]

That separation is an engineering asset. A failure in geometry should lead to geometry evidence; a failure in native input should lead to native evidence. Treating every visible problem as a core defect, or every passing core check as approval of the object, would erase the useful boundary.
Supported now does not mean universally compatible

Workstream 114 later changed the current product status: BowserBOY DS is a supported console, not a feature currently labeled “local prototype.” The change reconciled UI labels, runtime errors and documentation, and its public-copy verification was recorded through the monitored release. It did not add emulator functionality or certify additional games. Historical captions, filenames and work logs deliberately retained their provenance. [S2]

Thus both statements can be true: the first delivery was a local prototype; the current product presents DS as supported. The old workstream's open device/aesthetic qualifications are not evidence that current UI should still call it a prototype. Equally, removing that label cannot turn a desktop viewport check into a physical-device performance result.

The current acceptance boundary is concrete. Authorized, uncompressed .nds files must have an original-DS header, valid ARM program ranges and a size between 512 bytes and 512 MiB. DSi-enhanced and DSi-only inputs are rejected. The runtime options select stacked screens, no gap, 256×192 internal LCD resolution and one core, with external BIOS and BIOS-menu boot disabled. These are configuration and validation facts, not a promise that every structurally valid cartridge boots. [S3, S4]

Direct boot trades a simpler static-hosted launch for a compatibility boundary. Twin Lab demonstrates one BIOS-free path. It does not show that every game's startup assumptions are satisfied. The guide says this explicitly and distinguishes supplied user cartridges from automated fixtures. A maintainer should preserve that wording even after a particular user-supplied opening has appeared in public media. [S4]
Follow ownership through the selection boundary
Figure ND01-01. The console boundary follows cartridge identity and lifecycle, not merely the selected model's color.

The diagram combines the immediate-loading contract with the established lifecycle contract. DS play appears before full-file reading and hashing, so a slow identification step no longer leaves the cartridge sidebar as the only apparent response. The lower LCD supplies loading feedback; reduced motion keeps that graphic static. None of this accelerates the runtime download. It makes pending work legible and preserves cancellation and rejection behavior. [S5]

Persistence is equally part of the console identity. The DS has its own database and checksummed .bbds-save backups. Switching checkpoints and pauses the inactive runtime; simultaneous emulation was not required by the original acceptance contract. Power-on cold boot and same-ROM reload recovery are intentionally different operations. Without that distinction, “resume” could accidentally become a promise that a checkpoint survives replacement by a newer live-session save. Workstream 79 records an actual correction to that mistaken testing expectation. [S1]
ND01-W01 - Read a successful boot without overclaiming

Suppose the original Twin Lab demo boots and a mark appears on the lower physical LCD after touch input. A useful receipt identifies the fixture, runtime version, native output and displayed output. It supports the claim that this input-to-display path worked in that environment.

Now consider the next inference: “Any accepted .nds file will work.” The inference fails because header validation establishes structure, not the behavior of all programs accepted by that structure. The implementation hashes the full file to identify it only after header checks; it does not execute a compatibility proof. [S3]

Similarly, a 390-pixel desktop-browser layout result supports responsive framing, not physical-phone latency or thermal behavior. A later successful Pages gate establishes the retained hosted scenarios at its exact revision. It cannot retroactively qualify every prototype scenario, particularly the 21 cases still explicitly parked at this book's cutoff. [S1, S6]
ND01-R01 - Retry the boundary, not the whole product

Workstream 115 provides a practical retry model. A rejected replacement must report its error without losing an existing DS session; a cancelled native startup must stop loading and leave a usable retry route. The recorded focused cases exercised held upload reading, native handoff, invalid replacement retention, reduced motion and cancellation. [S5]

Preserve the last valid ownership state while retrying the failed operation. A loading animation is useful precisely because it does not pretend those states are already successful.

ND02 / THE DEVELOPMENT JOURNEY
The development journey
Which failed hypothesis should change the design?

A DS on a physical-looking desk has several clocks and coordinate systems: pointer events, native input polling, framebuffer copying, scene rendering and GPU completion. The motivating question is how to determine which one failed without compensating in the wrong layer. This chapter's outcome is a causal reading of the journey, not a catalog of commits.
The account is pinned to 61845372142b41992916f3732ea102cc0f4c8edf. Historical measurements below are receipts from the public record, not newly executed benchmarks.
From a second object to an articulated console

Workstream 79 established dual-screen output, native input and separate persistence, then reopened the model after rejection of its geometry, hinge and loose stylus. Its correction log also records pickup intersection, frozen inspection paints, scaled framebuffer splitting and lower-LCD direct-color behavior. These were different failures with different owners; a single “DS implemented” milestone would hide their causes. [S1]

Subsequent numbered workstreams refined the object into an interaction system. Independent console movement made placement a constraint rather than a fixed coordinate. Articulated inspection and locked gameplay orientation meant the same touchscreen had to remain accurate through body rotation, hinge motion, zoom and resizing. A picked-up pen then had to remain visually useful without blocking its own input ray. These dependencies explain why touch correctness could not be reduced to a single screenshot in the initial flat pose. [S2, S3]

Not every numbered idea became a feature. The boxed-cartridge library remained explicitly deferred and required title-specific redistribution permission. A physical cartridge prop therefore must not be narrated as a downloadable game catalog. The book selects these causal boundaries rather than exporting every intermediate tracking entry. [S4]
A pointer offset was not permission to move every touch

Workstream 88 began with a click near the lower-right LCD appearing substantially higher in Twin Lab. The tempting repair would have shifted host coordinates. Instead, the recorded investigation traced the native bridge and original homebrew, corrected the demo's Y conversion and restricted brush bounds, and retained physical UV mapping. Native corner tests separately exposed synthetic autofocus/blur behavior and inclusive viewport endpoint issues. [S5]

That distinction protects every other cartridge from a compensation for one fixture's bug. Physical antialiasing introduced another false signal: a corner between drawing-buffer pixels could not reasonably be required to contain one completely yellow pixel. The corrected probe used a small sampling footprint while retaining exact native brush assertions. This was fixture accuracy, not permission to accept arbitrary drawing offsets.

Quick taps then falsified a different assumption. Eight ordinary clicks lost marks even though coordinates were correct; down/up arrived only 0–0.3 ms apart. Earlier held-contact precision tests had not exercised that path. Two browser animation frames still lost touches. The pinned native frame counter demonstrated why: browser paint boundaries are not native input-poll boundaries. The repair retained contact edges across actual native frame changes, coalesced pending moves and discarded queued contacts on cancellation. [S5]
Figure ND02-01. A correct coordinate, a registered native contact and a timely displayed mark are three different observations.
Correct pixels can still arrive too late

The touch story did not end when native marks became correct. The public record contains software-rendered runs where native and copied pixels were right only after the unchanged 1500 ms quick-tap deadline. It also records a cached-controller experiment that failed and was rejected. A pass on hardware did not invalidate that software result. [S6]

Resize exposed another layer: camera positions changed while inverse and world matrices waited for an eligible room paint. A deferred-paint phone regression mapped (32,80) to (65,56) before correction. Synchronizing camera and active-model matrices at the change fixed projection without waiting for GPU rendering. A later held-pen regression showed that projected controls also needed synchronization after resize. [S6]

There was no evidence for a universal “GPU problem” that excused every failure. The record distinguishes delayed evaluation, native contact loss, stale projection and copying gated by room paints. An unqualified tiled/snapshot overlay experiment was removed because it still failed and exposed transition state before its full frame completed. Minimal full-frame fences and independent native-half copying were retained. The engineering trade-off was to decouple necessary work without publishing an incompletely rendered state. [S6]
ND02-W01 - Light the shell by moving the shell

Workstream 116 is a compact example of testing a physical explanation. The upright pose at (5,5.1,8) placed the front shell ahead of the lamp's emitting region. Lamp-only blue samples were only 9 on the lid and 10 on the deck. Enlarging tabletop bounce alone was ineffective.

Moving toward the light was promising but not sufficient: the first target (-2,5.1,-2) failed full-rotation clearance with a recorded gap of -1.047. The bounded correction moved the shared target to (-2,5.1,-8). Final physical-shell samples reached blue 108–113 on the lid and 117–157 on the deck; all eight sampled rays hit shell and went black with every lamp off. No material, light or exposure edit was needed. [S7]

This result answers the original readability complaint without inventing a camera light or brightening native LCDs. Earlier paint work had already shown why hex-only trials were insufficient: rendered shell color depended on reflection and illumination, and measurements had to exclude green LCD pixels. Readability was a spatial problem here, not another request to repaint the console. [S8]
ND02-R01 - Retry a fixture without rewriting the observation

The new lighting fixture initially treated powered-off reflective glass as an unlit LCD. Its bounded repair used actual static status LCDs; native screen/input behavior remained separately qualified. Similarly, workstream 115 found full-file digest and storage lookup occurring before sidebar closure. Moving visible play/loading feedback earlier addressed perceived inactivity without claiming faster emulation. [S7, S9]

A useful retry changes the falsified assumption and preserves the question's original strength. It does not enlarge every deadline, lower renderer sharpness or reclassify a late result as timely. Later CI parking therefore remains unresolved evidence debt even where focused local checks succeeded.

ND03 / STATIC HOST, NATIVE CORE
Static host, native core

Question: how does a static website become a DS without a game server? Outcome: trace a cartridge from a local browser file to a native emulator, and distinguish an application boundary from a security sandbox.
The host does not emulate the processors

BowserBOY DS combines a browser application, a Three.js physical presentation and a pinned EmulatorJS 4.2.3 adapter using DeSmuME. It is not a new ARM9 or ARM7 emulator. The website supplies the appliance around that existing core: cartridge selection, power, checked storage, input routing, scene geometry, status and recoverable errors.

Static hosting serves HTML, JavaScript and assets. The browser executes the application and emulator locally. The selected cartridge becomes a browser File, not an upload to a game-processing server. That distinction does not make first launch offline: src/player.js fetches the pinned runtime loader and its dependencies from the EmulatorJS CDN. CDN access is a real dependency. There is no service-worker-backed, guaranteed offline installation contract.
Figure ND03-01. Execution ownership. The CDN supplies runtime code; it is not the owner of local checkpoints or a remote gameplay service.
Three boundaries, three different promises

DsController owns the physical DS session. It knows the selected cartridge, checkpoint store, iframe, visible controls, screen materials and current power/pause state. It does not spread upstream EJS_emulator internals through the scene.

player.js is the version-sensitive adapter. It translates host commands into the pinned runtime's APIs, configures native options, retains the WebGL drawing buffer and translates native results back into messages. An upstream change therefore has a bounded inspection surface, although a version pin alone does not prove continued CDN availability.

The same-origin iframe separates document layout and runtime lifecycle from the desk. It is deliberately readable by the host, which obtains the native canvas through contentDocument. This is not a hostile-code security boundary. Same-origin code and downloaded runtime dependencies remain trusted code. Calling it a sandbox would overstate what the implementation provides.
Session identity is not optional decoration

The host creates a new UUID at launch. A host message handler accepts an event only when its source is the current iframe window, its origin matches the page and its session matches the current session UUID. The adapter likewise requires the parent window, matching origin and valid session. Initialization also checks that the ROM is a Blob and the game identity is a 64-digit lowercase hexadecimal digest.

These checks solve a practical asynchronous problem: an old runtime must not finish a command against a replacement cartridge. They do not authenticate arbitrary same-origin scripts or provide a capability boundary against all compromised page code.

Requests have separate UUIDs. pending, a Map, associates each command with its resolve/reject callbacks and ten-second timer. A result settles only its matching entry. clear() rejects pending work and removes the iframe; it does not leave callers waiting for results from a destroyed runtime.
ND03-W01 - A capture round trip

The Save action calls command('capture'). The controller registers the pending request before posting the message. The adapter validates the session, calls getState() and getSaveFile(), validates the resulting DS capture and sends a bba:result with the request ID.

The controller clears the timer and resolves the matching promise. Only then does the host attempt the IndexedDB transaction. Native capture and durable storage are separate steps: a successful capture is not a successful save. The save chapter follows that distinction through failure.
Failure is a message, not a blank screen

Loader download failure, invalid native video dimensions and runtime errors are surfaced as explicit failure messages. Launch has a 90-second deadline and a visible Cancel action. Post-start failure clears the runtime, powers the controller down and opens the cartridge tools with an error.

The adapter disables its own databases/local storage and hides unmanaged save/import controls. This avoids two competing persistence owners. It is not a blanket claim that every possible upstream feature is audited.
ND03-R01 - Replace the session before a result returns

Suppose request A belongs to a removed iframe, and cartridge B is now active. Even a well-formed delayed response from A cannot pass the current-window and session checks. The old promise is already rejected by clear(). A request ID without source/session checking would not provide that protection.
ND03-Q01 - Why not call DeSmuME directly from the scene?
ND03-A01 - Contain the unstable interface

Direct calls would make rendering and physical interaction depend on version-specific emulator internals and its document lifetime. The adapter centralizes that coupling; messages give operations explicit completion and error paths. This improves maintainability, not automatic compatibility with future EmulatorJS versions.

ND04 / CARTRIDGE, LOADING AND POWER
Cartridge, loading and power
Question: what should happen immediately after selecting a large ROM? Outcome: distinguish scene handoff, validation, insertion, native launch, checkpoint resume, pause and power cycling.
Give the player the console before doing expensive work

The important loading improvement is ordering, not a fictional speedup. load(file) closes the DS tools, selects DS, requests playing view and paints READING LOCAL ROM before awaiting cartridge identification. Large-file reading, hashing and native startup still take time, but the player is no longer stranded in the selection sidebar without visible progress.

This is asynchronous work on the page, not a claim that the ROM hashing was moved to a worker. Reading bytes and computing a digest can consume memory and browser resources. The observable contract is early handoff and a loading display while awaited work proceeds; it is not instant emulation.
Figure ND04-01. The handoff happens before ROM identification. The loading animation communicates a phase, not measured percentage completion.
Validation has a declared compatibility boundary

identifyDsRom accepts an uncompressed .nds filename, requires at least 512 bytes and caps the file at 512 MiB. It reads a 512-byte header and rejects nonzero unit-code byte 0x12, so DSi-enhanced and DSi-only files are outside this implementation's accepted input scope.

For each ARM program descriptor at 0x20 and 0x30, it checks ROM offset, entry address, load address and length. Program bytes must lie in the file; the load range must lie within the accepted memory ranges; the normalized entry must fall inside that program. These checks catch malformed/truncated files before loading a large native runtime.

They are not a full DS cartridge authenticity or compatibility verifier. A valid descriptor does not prove that a particular game's timing, peripherals or save behavior work in the browser. The full file digest identifies checkpoint ownership; the display title comes from the filename, with underscores replaced and the extension removed.
Two loading visuals solve different problems

The physical cartridge moves from y = 3.1 toward its seated y = .44. The insertion clock accumulates actual painted elapsed time over 1800 ms, using smoothstep t*t*(3-2*t) rather than treating a frame count as time. These are local model coordinates, not browser-screen coordinates or a claim about a standard retail shell. Chapter 08 distinguishes the actual modeled slots from the media caption's description of insertion.

The lower LCD separately draws a small original card animation and three progress dots. Its twelve-frame sequence changes on 160 ms buckets. It continues through reading and native startup, then yields to the real framebuffer. It is drawn into a canvas texture rather than fetched as an external GIF, so it remains integrated with the physical display.

With reduced motion, the cartridge is immediately seated and the loading display stays on frame zero. Status still communicates that work is happening. Reduced motion must remove unnecessary motion, not remove the information.
ND04-W01 - Selecting a cartridge with an existing checkpoint

The controller first identifies the file. If another cartridge is running, it saves that session before replacing it. The selected ROM's digest looks up a DS checkpoint. After clearing the previous runtime, the controller stores the new File, identity and any battery bytes in memory, begins insertion and launches with the matching checkpoint.

On game start, the adapter loads battery data and native state, then waits for rendered frames before acknowledging readiness. The host checks both native dimensions and the actual retained canvas before replacing loading materials with live outputs. A loaded iframe by itself is not a running DS.
Power is not pause, and resume is not a fresh boot

Pause retains the running runtime and asks it to stop advancing. Switching away from a running, unpaused DS uses suspend(): release inputs, save when storage is available, pause and remember that this was an automatic suspension. Returning resumes that retained runtime only if it was suspended. An intentionally paused DS should not become unpaused merely because the player switches consoles.

Power off saves first when running, then clears the runtime, marks power off and installs dark physical screen materials. The selected cartridge stays in memory. Power on launches a new runtime with battery data, not the old native checkpoint. The adapter writes the battery bytes and restarts the core, preserving the distinction between an in-game save and a resumed machine snapshot.
Initial cartridge selection may resume a checkpoint; deliberate power cycling boots from the in-game save. Neither operation persists the ROM itself across a page reload.
ND04-R01 - Storage fails while powering off

togglePower() awaits save() before clearing a running runtime. If durable storage is unavailable, the save throws with instructions to export. The operation wrapper displays the error and opens tools instead of reporting a successful safe shutdown. The same choice protects against replacing a running cartridge after a failed save.
The application cannot guarantee recovery after browser termination, storage eviction or a user ignoring an export warning. The next chapter on saves explains the portable escape route.
ND04-Q01 - Does a seated cartridge prove that startup succeeded?
ND04-A01 - Animation and execution are separate clocks

No. Insertion can finish while the runtime download is still pending. Native success requires a started message and a valid retained display. Conversely, reduced-motion insertion can be instantaneous without altering startup. Treating a visual transition as proof of execution would hide real failures.

ND05 / ONE FRAMEBUFFER, TWO LIVE SCREENS
One framebuffer, two live screens

Question: how do two physical LCDs show one emulator without two cores? Outcome: trace the video contract, integer scaling, texture sampling, loading replacement and the distinction between screen brightness and light.
Make the native layout explicit

The native DS picture is two 256 by 192 screens. The adapter configures DeSmuME for top/bottom layout, zero gap and native internal resolution. After startup it checks the core's reported video dimensions: exactly 256 by 384. This prevents a swapped, horizontal or gapped layout from silently producing plausible but incorrect crops.

The actual presentation canvas may be integer-scaled. dsScreenRegions accepts widths from 256 through 2048, divisible by 256, with height exactly 1.5 times width. It returns equal upper/lower rectangles. These two checks operate at different layers: native dimensions describe the core; canvas dimensions describe its presentation surface.
Figure ND05-01. Two views of one running native framebuffer. No second emulator and no independent screen clocks are created.
Retention is an initialization requirement

WebGL does not generally promise that a drawing buffer remains readable after presentation. During runtime setup, the adapter wraps only that core canvas's WebGL getContext call to request preserveDrawingBuffer: true. On bba:started, the host verifies that the actual context reports that attribute. A missing retained buffer fails visibly rather than becoming intermittent black LCDs.

This is a performance trade-off: retention and copying can cost memory and GPU bandwidth. It is not a globally applied WebGL override, and changing the attribute after a context has been created is not equivalent to asking for it when the context is first constructed.
ND05-W01 - An integer-scaled canvas

Suppose the canvas is 512 by 768. Validation accepts it: width is twice 256, height is 1.5 times width. The upper rectangle is (0,0,512,384) and the lower is (0,384,512,384). Each is drawn into a separate 256 by 192 output canvas.

imageSmoothingEnabled = false avoids an extra 2D interpolation pass. The Three.js maps use nearest minification and magnification filters with no mipmaps. paintScreens() marks the maps dirty after copying. These choices preserve crisp source pixels; they do not increase native detail or make a 256-pixel-wide source equivalent to higher-resolution emulation.
The screen is not a lamp-lit plastic surface

Live LCD materials are MeshBasicMaterial with toneMapped: false, rather than ordinary shell materials whose visibility depends on the desk lamp. The game remains visible when room lamps are off. Shell highlights, surrounding light spill and framebuffer content remain separate concerns.

Before native video exists, status and loading pictures use host-generated canvas textures. drawLcdCrt provides their built-in presentation treatment. The controller's DS preferences disable the native shader by default. When the native framebuffer arrives, it replaces the temporary display materials; the implementation does not stack the pre-cartridge treatment on top of the live native picture.

No CRT presentation is proof of timing accuracy. Likewise, a changing pool of light on the desk is not proof that the emulated game accepted input. Pixel evidence, light evidence and input evidence need different checks.
What goes wrong when the contract drifts?

A horizontal canvas can still contain colorful output, but splitting it vertically would duplicate or scramble its screens. A gap changes the touch-to-picture correspondence. A noninteger scale changes the assumptions behind crisp downsampling. dsScreenRegions rejects these shapes explicitly.

During screen copying, an unexpected error is reported to the player, the source is detached and tools are opened for recovery. The application does not manufacture a static fallback and call it a live frame.
ND05-R01 - Introduce a 20-pixel gap

A 256 by 404 canvas fails the required geometry. Removing that check would require redesigning both crops and lower-screen coordinate dispatch, not merely tolerating a different height. The safe small change is to retain the pinned zero-gap runtime configuration, not guess the content boundary.
ND05-Q01 - Can two different screen colors establish full DS compatibility?
ND05-A01 - It establishes a narrower fact

Different, advancing screen output can establish a functioning split in a particular fixture or game. It does not establish save behavior, native touch positions, every title's timing or performance on phones. Verification must name the input, environment and contract it actually observes.

ND06 / TOUCH, CONTROLS AND THE STYLUS
Touch, controls and the stylus
Question: why is a DS tap more than a click on a rectangle? Outcome: trace a screen coordinate through a 3D ray, UV coordinates, native contact edges and source-owned button state.
Find the visible surface, not an approximate box

The physical DS can rotate, change hinge angle and zoom. An axis-aligned DOM rectangle around its lower display cannot express that perspective or the lid's occlusion. touchAt(event) converts the pointer position relative to the renderer canvas into normalized device coordinates. A ray from the actual camera intersects the DS model.

The controller takes the first relevant hit and accepts it only if the object is the lower screen. A hit on the shell or covering lid is not a valid touch. When the held stylus is visible, its own marked geometry is excluded from this search. The pen must not block the LCD it is indicating.
Figure ND06-01. Every transformation has a defined coordinate system. Touch depends on actual visible geometry, not merely a projected bounding box.
UV conversion has a deliberate edge rule
dsTouchFromUv rejects missing, nonfinite or out-of-range coordinates. For accepted UV values, it computes:

x = min(255, floor(u * 256))
y = min(191, floor((1 - v) * 192))

The vertical flip connects mesh UV orientation to native top-left screen coordinates. The minimum prevents the inclusive UV endpoints from generating out-of-range pixel 256 or 192. Device-pixel ratio does not enter this formula: the DOM event and bounding rectangle use CSS pixels; the ray resolves the physical surface; the UV then resolves native pixels.

The adapter checks integer coordinates again. It maps the native point to the combined canvas using pixel centers, adding 192 to address the lower half. Its dispatch formula accounts for inclusive browser-driver viewport endpoints instead of landing on an offscreen edge.
A fast press and release must survive native polling
Browser tasks and emulator frames are different clocks. Posting down and up in adjacent message tasks can complete before the native core next polls input, producing no observed contact.

DsTouchQueue retains contact transitions. After dispatching a sample it awaits dsInputFrame, which waits until the core's frame number changes while the queue generation remains current. Consecutive movement samples can coalesce to the latest move; press and release boundaries are retained. The goal is not to replay every mouse move. It is to preserve the semantic edges of contact while keeping movement current.

Cancellation increments a generation, discards pending samples and sends a release when the last dispatched state was pressed. An older asynchronous flush cannot continue injecting a stroke after pause, restore, blur or console switching. This is a cancellation protocol, not a timeout-based guess that the core probably saw a click.
ND06-W01 - A quick tap followed by a drag

Consider samples down(20,30), up(20,30), down(80,90), move(90,95), move(100,100), up(100,100). The two moves can collapse to the latest coordinate, but the first tap's down/up and second contact's down/up remain distinct. The core receives an opportunity to advance between dispatched contact states.

If a modal opens during the stroke, inputAllowed() becomes false and input release/cancellation prevents a stuck stylus. A pointer leaving the valid lower-screen surface releases contact rather than drawing through the surrounding plastic.
A physical pen is a separate presentation

The held pen is a clone of the docked model. Its raycast function is disabled and it is added to the scene independently, leaving the original docked geometry in the model's bounds. The held visual points toward the camera with its tip placed on the ray intersection or a camera-facing plane.

The implementation lifts the tip along the pointer ray, not along the LCD normal. Moving along the ray preserves the projected cursor location; moving along the normal could visibly slide the pen tip away from the contact point. Returning the stylus, Escape, right-click, lost availability and blur have explicit cleanup. Visual pickup is not required for direct lower-screen touch.
Buttons have multiple legitimate owners

The adapter holds a Map from action to a Set of source IDs. Keyboard and pointer can hold the same action simultaneously. Native press state changes only when the set crosses empty/nonempty. Releasing one owner cannot cancel another owner's held direction.

DS keys are arrows for directions, Z/X for A/B, A/S for Y/X, Q/W for L/R, Enter for Start and left Shift for Select. The DS-specific mapping is declared in DS_CONTROLS; it should not be inferred from another console's controls. DOM button targets are projected from actual control anchors, hidden when back-facing or covered and disabled outside playing input availability.
ND06-R01 - Blur before the queued release

On blur, release host inputs, return the stylus and cancel native queued contact. Merely clearing the JavaScript array would be insufficient if the native core already saw down. Cancellation must dispatch a release for that last delivered state as well.
ND06-Q01 - Why not coalesce the entire touch queue?
ND06-A01 - Latest position and contact history are different data

Replacing all pending samples with the newest one could turn a complete quick tap into an unpressed final coordinate. Coalescing adjacent moves removes redundant positions without erasing down/up edges. That distinction is the central input invariant, and the original Twin Lab fixture tests it through native observations rather than a decorative painted marker alone.

ND07 / SAVES, IDENTITY AND RECOVERY
Saves, identity and recovery

Question: which kind of progress survives which kind of interruption? Outcome: distinguish battery data, native checkpoints, browser storage and portable backups, including the failures each does not solve.
Four objects, not one vague save

An in-game save is the cartridge's battery-backed data, exposed as sram by the adapter. A checkpoint also contains the native core's machine state, so it can resume a running situation rather than boot normally. IndexedDB is the browser's origin-local storage location for the latest checkpoint. A .bbds-save file is the exported portable envelope containing checkpoint and optional battery data.

These are different layers. A downloaded backup is not automatic cloud sync. An IndexedDB transaction is not an immutable external copy. Loading battery bytes is not equivalent to loading the native state. The ROM is not stored inside either checkpoint or portable backup.
Figure ND07-01. Identity and validation precede persistence or restoration. The two storage routes have independent durability and user responsibilities.
Identity includes the complete cartridge

The host computes the full ROM digest. DsSaveStore keys records by DS_RUNTIME + ':' + digest, where the runtime marker is emulatorjs-4.2.3-desmume. Stored records repeat both runtime and ROM identity, and reads reject incompatible values.

Two files with the same title but different bytes must not share a checkpoint automatically. A title is a label, not a safe identity. Likewise, a future runtime upgrade must not quietly reinterpret old native states. The current marker provides a compatibility boundary; migration requires an explicit future design rather than a renamed string.

The database is bowserboy-ds, version 1, with a checkpoints object store. It is a separate DS store, not a second view of another console's records. Blocked/open failure is surfaced after a bounded wait. A late successful open after timeout closes its connection instead of reviving an abandoned operation. Version changes close the old connection.
Completion belongs to the transaction

put validates capture shape and size, then writes state, battery data, identity and timestamp in one readwrite transaction. The wrapper resolves on tx.oncomplete, not merely request success. A transaction can still abort after a request returns successfully.

Native state must be a nonempty Uint8Array of at most 64 MiB. Battery data is either null or a Uint8Array no larger than 16 MiB. null means no battery file; an empty byte array is a distinct valid byte sequence. Preserving that distinction matters when reconstructing an export.

Autosave runs every 30 seconds only while running, unpaused, not busy and storage is available. It is not a promise that every last moment survives a crash. The host warns before leaving a running session, but browser termination and eviction cannot be made safe by a warning alone.
ND07-W01 - Reading a portable backup

The first eight bytes are ASCII magic BBDS0001; the next four contain a little-endian metadata length. UTF-8 JSON follows, then state bytes and optional battery bytes. Metadata carries runtime, ROM identity, payload lengths and hashes. The battery length uses -1 for null.

The decoder bounds total file size before reading, checks magic, caps JSON at 4096 bytes and checks that metadata fits. It parses JSON, checks exact runtime/ROM identity, validates integer lengths and requires the complete envelope length to match. It then slices the payloads, applies DS capture limits and verifies hashes before returning anything eligible for restore.
total bytes = 12 + metadata bytes + state bytes + max(0, battery bytes)

This equality rejects both truncation and trailing unexpected payload. Hashes detect accidental corruption relative to the envelope; they are not a cryptographic signature proving who authored the file.
Restore deliberately crosses two boundaries

Import first decodes and validates the backup against the selected ROM. The player confirms replacing the current session/checkpoint. Where storage is available, the host persists the imported capture before requesting native restore. The adapter loads battery data, calls native loadState and waits for rendered frames before acknowledging restoration. If the runtime had been paused, it restores that pause afterward.

This is not a distributed transaction between IndexedDB and a native core. An IndexedDB commit followed by a native restore error can leave the imported checkpoint persisted while the live runtime did not complete restoration. The implementation surfaces the error; the book should not invent atomic rollback across those components.
Failed persistence must not look successful

If persistence throws, storageAvailable becomes false and the player is told to export before leaving. Saving updates the in-memory battery copy from the native capture, but that does not make the browser record durable. Power-off and cartridge replacement wait for save, so a failed save prevents those normal operations from silently destroying the running session.

Export directly captures the running core and requests a download. It can therefore be useful even when browser storage is unavailable. The application reports a download request, not proof that the operating system saved the file or that a user later tested it on another machine.
ND07-R01 - Rename a ROM and import its backup

If only the filename changes, identical bytes retain the same digest, so identity remains valid. Change one byte and the digest changes; the previous backup must be rejected even when the filename remains identical. This is why a user-visible name is not the storage key.
ND07-Q01 - Is a checksum a guarantee that a backup will always restore?
ND07-A01 - Integrity is narrower than compatibility

No. The decoder proves the selected envelope's structural and checksum conditions under the pinned format/runtime identity. It does not prove all future runtime versions, every title's native state behavior, permanent storage or absence of failures during restoration. Exported copies and careful version boundaries reduce risk without removing it.

ND08 / THE DS ON THE DESK
The DS on the desk

The DS becomes convincing when its parts obey the same spatial story. A lid must carry its own screen when it folds. A saved playing angle must not erase the owner's tabletop arrangement. A lamp must illuminate the shell from its actual position, not merely make a screenshot brighter. This chapter explains those contracts at source cutoff 61845372142b41992916f3732ea102cc0f4c8edf. Source inspection here is not a new browser run, physical-device qualification or human visual approval.
One body, two transform spaces

createDsHandheld() builds original procedural geometry, not a photograph wrapped around a box. The root owns the lower shell, controls, battery cover, card and stylus. The upper shell and upper LCD belong to a separate lid group. Rotating that group changes the upper half without moving the lower touchscreen. The segmented barrel and collars make the joint legible, but the articulation is a bounded transform, not simulated hinge torque.

The two screen planes measure 4.5 by 3.375 model units: the same 4:3 aspect as each 256-by-192 LCD. Surrounds, recesses and controls are separate geometry. That separation matters in Inspect: a screen-sized colored rectangle cannot stand in for a bezel, and a projected button target must follow its real anchor rather than a remembered screen coordinate. See the model construction, screens and hinge.

Rear details are equally structural. Two centered square holes are cut into the extruded outer lid, with inset floors behind them. The supplied DS emblem occupies a lower-body underside plane beside the right battery cover; it therefore does not swing with the lid. Four pale-green square pads, screw recesses and top-edge shoulder housings distinguish the underside from the control deck. Enlarging the emblem preserves its aspect ratio rather than stretching artwork across the battery seam.

There is an important naming boundary around the bottom-facing slot. The model's front expansion slot sits along the lower edge of the upright base and rotates its slot face through 90 degrees. It is not the separately named rear DS game-card slot near the hinge. Nor does a README caption saying “slides in from below” establish the card's local-space trajectory: DsController.load() starts the card at local Y 3.1 and render() seats it at Y .44. These are distinct modeled features, not interchangeable evidence of a hardware connector. The front/underside/card geometry and controller's insertion setup and card animation are the authoritative descriptions.
Pose is a contract, not one rotation
Figure ND08-01. Table placement, Inspect articulation and the session-only gameplay lock are separate state; returning to the table restores its resting hinge.

setDsHinge() accepts only finite values and only edits an unlocked DS in Inspect outside a transition. The opening is clamped to 30–180 degrees; the stored lid rotation is 180 - opening. Thus 180 degrees means zero lid rotation, while the table's 70-degree rotation represents a 110-degree opening. Confusing opening angle with stored rotation reverses an otherwise plausible slider.

setDsPoseLocked() clones the root quaternion and stores the lid rotation. It also clears active drag/pinch state, preventing an old gesture from continuing across the lock boundary. setView() chooses the saved desk rotation for table mode, the current rotation for Inspect, or the locked rotation/default identity for play. A lock survives view changes within the session; reloading is not pose persistence.

The camera uses the actual articulated bounds, not a flat-console rectangle. dsPoseBounds() evaluates body and lid geometry under their respective candidate transforms. updateCameraTargets() lifts the resulting envelope above the desk and fits its width, height and depth, reserving additional space for the phone Inspect panel. Immediate matrix updates keep projected controls consistent before another eligible GPU paint. These mechanisms are visible in pose editing and bounds, camera fitting and view transitions. Fitting is not visibility: an extreme backward pose can fit perfectly while the lid hides a screen or control.

Figure ND08-02. Existing DS Inspect GIF. The book renderer embeds only its first-frame PNG still, not the hinge motion; the repository GIF retains the sequence. LCDs replay a recorded native opening, not responses to these scene actions. Print still: frame zero of the animated source; not motion evidence.
Clearance follows the interaction

The desk is not organized by hiding inconvenient objects. In focus mode, the active DS is an immovable obstacle for placement purposes: its playing angle must not yield to a decorative prop. The inactive console is placed next, followed by Pear and the axolotl, then loose desk objects. In table mode, companion positions receive priority before props and consoles. Returning from focus restores remembered companion XZ coordinates, then reconciles lower-priority objects.

resolveDeskClearance() first accumulates candidate placements. If any placement fails, it reports blocked space without applying that partial list. On the table it retries the two console orders, because greedily placing the narrower object can trap the wider one. A signature avoids repeating unchanged work. This is deterministic bounded rearrangement, not a globally optimal packing solver.

nearestDeskPosition() reduces vertically overlapping obstacle boxes to forbidden XZ rectangles expanded by the moving object's bounds and a .25-unit gap. Candidates lie at the desired coordinate or rectangle edges, clamped to the workspace. It chooses the nearest valid squared-distance candidate; a small floating-point tolerance keeps a legal edge legal. Conservative axis-aligned boxes can reject visually empty corners around a rotated DS, trading packing density for predictable separation. Read mode priorities and atomic application with the placement solver.
Light must move through real space

The metallic lid uses blue #0077FF; the lower shell uses lighter #40A0FF, with grain, roughness and clearcoat. Those values do not promise the same perceived blue under every warm source. Brightening a material to compensate for backlighting would change other views too.

Workstream 116 records the causal correction: the old upright target (5, 5.1, 8) stood ahead of the lamp's emitting region. A first candidate (-2, 5.1, -2) improved illumination but failed a rotation-clearance check. The final shared target is (-2, 5.1, -8). Moving the object rather than adding a camera light preserved the existing paint, exposure and dark-room behavior. These measurements are historical task evidence, not measurements repeated for this chapter.

Pear and the axolotl are light-bearing scene objects, not glowing stickers. The axolotl's point light is a child of its movable root, so its light pool follows translation. Scene setters change emitted material intensity and light intensity together; off means removing illumination, not merely darkening a button. DeskMotion supplies held/released motion, gravity and damped impacts. Pear adds expressive recovery; the smaller companion reuses the motion without pretending to share every facial animation. See companion brightness, axolotl light attachment and drop integration.

ND08-W01 — Work a pose change through the system

Starting in unlocked play, enter Inspect and set the opening to 120 degrees. The lid rotation becomes 60 degrees. Rotate the body, lock, then return to play: the quaternion and hinge should be retained while camera fitting uses the new envelope. Put down: the desk orientation and 110-degree opening return. This is a reasoned walkthrough, not a claimed execution. Its diagnostic value is separating three failures: wrong hinge conversion, overwritten desk placement, and camera framing based on stale bounds.
ND08-R01 — Retry with a changed condition

Now put a companion where the DS envelope needs clearance and repeat the transition. The focused DS should keep its pose while lower-priority placements yield. If no placement exists, spread objects out or reset a clear home; do not shrink the DS, disable depth testing or silently discard the lock. Then retry with every lamp off. Darkness is expected, not evidence that the corrected material reverted.
ND08-Q01 — Why not always move the DS to resolve a collision?

Because focus mode promises a stable chosen pose and usable projected controls. Moving that priority object would make a decorative collision change the user's playing composition. Table mode has different ownership and may legitimately relocate consoles. Neither policy guarantees that every crowded arrangement has a solution.

ND09 / ALGORITHMS AND DATA STRUCTURES
Algorithms and data structures

Question: which small algorithms make this appliance coherent? Outcome: reason about time, coordinates, ownership and memory without mistaking a familiar data structure for an automatic performance guarantee.
Complexity starts with a declared unit

Let R be ROM bytes, S native-state bytes, B battery bytes, q pending touch samples, h physical button actions and p active command requests. Costs below describe application-side work, not the native emulator's CPU accuracy or instruction throughput. Hashing and copying do not become free because their APIs are asynchronous.
Figure ND09-01. Four different invariants. Each algorithm protects a specific meaning, not a generic promise that the entire emulator becomes fast.
Full-file identity: pay once per selection

Cartridge identification reads and hashes the entire R-byte ROM after checking the header. Work is linear in file size. An ArrayBuffer for the file means application memory proportional to R; native loading and structured cloning may add further live copies or allocations. The book does not claim zero-copy loading or bound total memory by the ROM alone.

That cost buys exact byte identity rather than a heuristic such as title plus file size. The early scene handoff hides neither the cost nor errors: it gives the player a meaningful display while awaited work proceeds.
A queue preserves edges, not every pointer coordinate

DsTouchQueue.samples is an array. A new move can replace a pending move at the tail. Contact starts and ends append separately. A generation counter invalidates in-flight work during cancellation. Dispatch is serialized by flushing, and each delivered sample awaits native frame advancement.

Tail replacement is constant-size work; array shift() conventionally moves remaining indexed entries and can cost O(q). The important practical limit is that high-frequency adjacent moves coalesce. A long sequence of alternating taps is not given a strict fixed queue bound by this code. Calling it a constant-memory queue would be inaccurate.

A future ring buffer could improve dequeue behavior if measured workloads justify it. Such a change would still need to preserve contact edges, cancellation generations and error propagation. Data-structure substitution alone does not prove the semantic invariant.
ND09-W01 - Why a boolean cannot represent a button

Keyboard Right goes down, then a pointer presses Right. There are now two source IDs in the action's set. The native button was already down, so no second native edge is needed. Keyboard release leaves one source; native Right stays down. Pointer release empties the set and sends native up.

The adapter's Map<action, Set<source>> models exactly that ownership. Under conventional hash-table behavior, lookup/add/delete are expected constant time; worst-case engine guarantees should not be inferred from that notation. Releasing everything visits the actual stored sources.

One boolean would fail when the first owner released. A reference count would handle balanced edges but would be harder to make idempotent under duplicate source events. Source sets make ownership explicit.
Maps also correlate commands

pending maps each request UUID to callbacks and a timer. Results locate their own request rather than relying on message arrival order. Timeout removes the entry before rejecting. Session teardown clears timers, rejects every remaining promise and empties the map.

The map uses O(p) entries, not unlimited history. The controller's busy guard serializes ordinary operations, but the data structure itself is not a formal hard cap on all possible outstanding requests.
Coordinates: affine conversion followed by geometry

The pointer is normalized within the canvas to [-1,1] in X and Y. Raycasting resolves the first visible surface under the current camera. An accepted lower-screen UV becomes a native integer pixel with vertical flip and inclusive-edge clamping. The adapter then maps that pixel's center into the lower half of its combined canvas.

The scalar conversions are O(1). Ray traversal depends on scene geometry and Three.js behavior; the book does not claim that intersecting the model is constant time. More importantly, replacing that geometry query with a rectangle changes semantics, not just cost.
Elapsed-time motion and damped response

Insertion accumulates elapsed paint timestamps and uses smoothstep e(t) = t²(3 - 2t) for t clamped to [0,1]. At t=.5, e=.5; its endpoint slopes are zero, making the approach gentler than a constant velocity jump. A missed paint produces a larger next elapsed step rather than assuming a fixed number of frames.

D-pad pitch/yaw use signed opposing directions. Diagonal magnitude is normalized by max(1,hypot(x,y)), so holding two perpendicular directions does not multiply total tilt by square root of two. Exponential damping uses the measured delta and separate press/release response rates; tiny residual differences snap to target to stop unnecessary repainting.
Backup validation has linear payload costs

Portable decoding checks size and metadata first, then copies and hashes payloads. Work and memory are proportional to S+B, within the declared limits. A checksum is O(payload), not a constant-time header check. The bounded JSON header avoids trusting an arbitrary metadata length before basic envelope validation.
ND09-R01 - Increase display refresh without changing motion speed

At twice the browser paint frequency, a frame-count-based insertion finishes twice as fast. Elapsed-time accumulation retains the 1800 ms target, subject to when the browser actually paints. It cannot guarantee that suspended tabs render motion smoothly; it guarantees the target is expressed in time, not an assumed frame rate.
ND09-Q01 - Which optimization is safe without additional evidence?
ND09-A01 - None merely because it sounds cheaper

Replacing SHA-based identity with a title, touch edges with a latest-only sample or geometry with a bounding box changes correctness contracts. Measure costs first, preserve the invariant in focused tests and name any new compatibility boundary. Simpler code is valuable only when it preserves the meaning the current algorithm protects.

ND10 / DESIGN PRINCIPLES AND FAILURE BOUNDARIES
Design principles and failure boundaries

Question: which principles actually explain this implementation? Outcome: recognize useful boundaries and their limits without inventing a perfect architecture or attaching pattern names to every function.
Own the truth at one layer

The host owns checked storage and player-visible lifecycle. The adapter owns version-sensitive native calls. The physical model owns geometry and anchors. The native core owns emulated state and output.

This separation prevents two persistence engines from independently choosing which checkpoint to resume. It also keeps a scene transformation from becoming a cartridge reboot. The implementation is not perfectly decoupled: the controller directly reads the same-origin canvas, and projection requires knowledge of scene objects. Those are deliberate integration boundaries, not evidence that every dependency has disappeared.
Figure ND10-01. Ownership follows the operation, then verification follows its observable consequence. A source change alone does not close the final arrow.
Fail early where the assumptions become knowable

Header ranges can be checked before native startup. Session identity can be checked when a message arrives. Video layout can be checked only after the core exposes dimensions. Storage durability can be acknowledged only when its transaction completes.

Moving a check earlier is useful only when the necessary information exists. For example, an .nds extension cannot establish that the ARM program bytes fit in the file; a valid header cannot establish native video readiness. The design uses a chain of narrower checks rather than one mythical “validated ROM” boolean.
ND10-W01 - A corrupted checkpoint must not become a fresh start

Suppose a matching IndexedDB record contains invalid state bytes. A success-shaped fallback would silently ignore the record and start a new game. That would make the app appear operational while concealing lost progress.

The store instead validates identity and capture shape and throws on an invalid record. The operation wrapper reports the error and opens tools. The portable decoder likewise rejects a bad checksum before restoration. The visible result can be less convenient, but it does not pretend the requested recovery happened.
Preserve invariants through every entry point

Keyboard, pointer and runtime-focused input share source-owned button semantics. Pause, configure, restore and hidden visibility cancel native touch. Power off, replacing a cartridge and switching consoles must release inputs before changing the runtime's availability.

A feature that works through one button but leaves a second entry point with stale state is incomplete. This is why a stylus demonstration needs cancel/blur cases and why visual model rotation must be tested alongside touch coordinates, not as an unrelated aesthetic action.
Cancellation is a first-class state transition

The touch queue's generation distinguishes current work from stale asynchronous work. Launch cancellation rejects a pending launch callback. Session clear rejects outstanding commands. These mechanisms do not silently convert abandonment into success.

They also have different scopes. Cancelling native startup is not the same as aborting an already awaited full-file read. Invalidating queued touch is not the same as terminating the native runtime. Good documentation states which operation is cancellable instead of generalizing one Cancel button to the entire application.
Separate simulation, presentation and observation

A physical button can move without native input being accepted. An LCD can display replay footage without a running core reacting. A lamp can change the shell while the self-lit LCD remains readable. A passing fixture is not every commercial game's compatibility.

The book's source-backed diagrams explain implementation. The visual showcase demonstrates scene presentation with recorded opening replay. The original Twin Lab tests observe native contracts. Release receipts qualify a specific revision in a specific environment. None substitutes for all the others.
ND10-R01 - Upgrade the runtime

Treat an upgrade as a compatibility change, not a URL edit. Recheck game-manager APIs, framebuffer retention, dimension/layout settings, native touch polling and save-state behavior. A changed native state format may require a new runtime identity and explicit recovery guidance.

Reusing old hashes or old checkpoint metadata would not establish new compatibility. Preserve the old book and release evidence as dated records, then qualify the changed implementation independently.
ND10-Q01 - Does isolation mean that switching consoles cannot fail?
ND10-A01 - A boundary reduces coupling, not all failure

Separate sessions and stores prevent accidental shared-state ownership. Switching can still fail while saving, pausing, starting or accessing the CDN. The controller must report those failures and retain useful state where possible. Independence is an architectural property; successful switching is an observed operation with its own prerequisites.

ND12 / VISUAL DOCUMENTATION
Visual documentation

A DS showcase must make two screens, a hinged body and a small set of physical interactions understandable before a reader studies the guide. It must also say what was actually recorded. A beautifully timed button press beside moving LCD pixels can suggest a causal relationship that the capture does not contain. Good visual documentation controls that interpretation as carefully as it controls framing.

This chapter uses the public repository at 61845372142b41992916f3732ea102cc0f4c8edf. It explains the existing workflow, not a new capture session. Private cartridges, videos, timing receipts and browser stores were not needed to write it and are not book inputs.
The README is a front page, not the entire manual

The repository's GIF-first policy is explicit and local to this project. The front page offers motion and short captions; setup, detailed controls, limitations and release evidence live in linked documentation. This division is especially useful for DS: a hinge sequence communicates articulation quickly, while the 30–180-degree limit, session-only lock and occlusion rules require prose that should not interrupt every animation.

The documentation chain therefore has different jobs. The README attracts and orients. The guide tells a player how to act. MEDIA.md establishes capture provenance and interpretation. Public TODOs retain causal failures, acceptance criteria and qualification boundaries. This engineering book explains why those choices exist. Copying all five layers into the front page would make each layer harder to maintain.

The approved DS logo is artwork, not a native-game screenshot. Likewise, an image of a rear emblem documents branding placement, not cartridge compatibility. Workstreams 92 and 99 concern DS visual identity; 95, 100 and 103 concern physical markings. Keeping those claims separate prevents an attractive identity treatment from becoming accidental runtime evidence. The controlling policy and current edition are recorded in MEDIA.md, opening edition.
Two timelines, one scene
Figure ND12-01. Native LCD acquisition and live scene manipulation meet only in the capture harness; their coexistence does not prove that the game responds to the depicted controls.

The current edition records the selected DS opening for 90 native seconds, then excludes its first eight seconds. Native time begins at entry to EJS_onGameStart, after core/cartridge loading, not at page navigation and not at a later host-ready notification. The recorder intercepts the served player source in an isolated browser context and captures the native canvas. The DS row explicitly selects 90 seconds and an eight-second trim. See native acquisition hook.

That recording then becomes a source for a second operation. openingReplay() serves private opening videos through intercepted browser routes, creates off-DOM video/canvas pairs, and exposes the DS canvas through an instance-specific source accessor. Browser actions still operate real scene controls; the screen image is supplied by the recording. Geometry, materials and lighting are not replaced with a composited illustration. The implementation boundary is explicit in the replay installation and receipt declaration.

Consequently, a DS button GIF establishes physical button travel while an untouched opening plays. A stylus GIF establishes pickup and scene tracing, not native touchscreen response to that trace. A lighting GIF establishes scene light changes with recorded LCD content. Those are useful, honest demonstrations. Calling them live game-input demonstrations would be false, even though the source pixels originally came from a running native core. Capture-only replay must not become a shipping-player fallback.

Four different kinds of evidence

Local integrity answers whether files decode, have expected dimensions, durations and loop flags, and differ across temporal samples. A changing sample does not show that every frame is correctly framed.

Bounded visual review answers whether inspected frames show the intended state. The recorded workflow caught an axolotl panel hiding its lamp and a settings sequence missing its drawer. Replacing those takes addressed specific observed failures, not every possible visual defect.

Hosted qualification answers whether the exact source passed its delivery gate. MEDIA.md records that the opening-media commit's Pages run failed an unchanged fullscreen case and skipped deployment, followed by a bounded fixture correction and successful later deployment. Public GIF byte checks were a separate result. A reachable GitHub image did not retroactively turn the failed Pages run green.

Human approval concerns whether the owner accepts the appearance and editorial choices. Neither an empty browser error array nor a successful deployment supplies that judgment. The historical successful run still retained 21 existing skipped browser scenarios; this chapter creates no new test result or compatibility claim. See the publication record.
ND12-W01 — Write the caption from the evidence

Suppose the selected artifact is ds-inspect.gif. First identify the demonstrated mechanism: body rotation, hinge change and pose locking. Next identify the LCD source: the current edition's replayed native opening. Finally identify the destination: animated repository page or first-frame book still.

A defensible caption is: “DS body and hinge inspection with a session pose lock; recorded opening on the LCDs.” In the book, append the first-frame limitation. Do not write “the game responds while the player folds the DS.” That sentence would require separate live native-input evidence.
ND12-R01 — Retry after the condition changes

Now assume the GIF is valid but a controls panel covers the lamp during the brightness change. Decoding it again cannot repair the composition. In an authorized future capture, dismiss or reposition the panel through the real UI, retake the affected sequence, then repeat temporal review and integrity checks. Do not paint over the panel or substitute a brighter render.

If publication alone fails, preserve the distinction: verify the exact source and delivery gate rather than recording replacement footage to fix an unrelated hosted assertion. The present chapter performs neither retry; it specifies the decision rule.
ND12-Q01 — Does the book still prove that the light followed the lamp?

No. One frame can show a lamp and an illuminated region together. Motion requires the original sequence or separate temporal evidence. The source also explains that the light is attached to the movable root, but source structure is not a substitute for human review of the animation.

Run the smallest relevant command
The application requires Node 22 or newer and its existing locked dependencies. From the repository root:

npm run build
npm run check

ND13-W01 - Change touch-edge rounding

First inspect dsTouchFromUv and its unit cases. Predict UV zero, UV one, mid-screen and nonfinite/out-of-range behavior. Then inspect adapter dispatchTouch: its combined-canvas pixel-center rule is a second transformation, not a duplicate of the first.

Run focused unit cases, then the native pointer scenarios needed by the change: quick tap, held pen, changed orientation, zoom and high-DPI touch. Record any parked cases explicitly. A center-point screenshot alone cannot qualify an edge-rounding change.
